domanda: Contoso plans to use Azure Backup to protect an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server and a container in an Azure Blob Storage account. Both resources are located in the East US region. You need to identify the minimum vault configuration required to protect both datasources. What should you create?
opzione_a: One Recovery Services vault in East US
opzione_b: One Backup vault in East US
opzione_c: One Recovery Services vault and one Backup vault in East US
opzione_d: Two Recovery Services vaults in East US, one per datasource type
spiegazione: Correct (b): Azure Backup supports two vault types that target different datasources. A Backup vault (Microsoft.DataProtection/BackupVaults) is the vault used for the newer workloads, and its supported datasources include Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL server, and Kubernetes services. Because both an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server and Azure Blobs are Backup vault datasources, a single Backup vault in the same region as the resources is sufficient. (a) is wrong: a Recovery Services vault supports Azure VMs, SQL in Azure VM, Azure Files, SAP HANA in Azure VM, MARS agent, Azure Backup Server (MABS), and DPM - it cannot protect PostgreSQL servers or Blobs. (c) is wrong: it is unnecessary, because neither datasource requires a Recovery Services vault; the requirement asks for the minimum configuration. (d) is wrong: it doubles the wrong vault type; Recovery Services vaults do not support either of these datasources, and a single vault can hold multiple datasource types anyway.
tags: azure backup,backup vault,recovery services vault,postgresql,blob backup,vault types

domanda: A colleague creates a Recovery Services vault named RSV1 by accepting all the default settings. Your company does not use Azure as its primary backup storage endpoint, so RSV1 must store its backup data in locally-redundant storage to reduce cost. When can you change the storage replication type of RSV1?
opzione_a: At any time. Azure Backup automatically migrates the existing recovery points to the new replication type.
opzione_b: Only before a backup is configured in the vault.
opzione_c: Only after the first backup job has completed successfully.
opzione_d: Only while the vault contains no backup policies.
spiegazione: Correct (b): Microsoft Learn explicitly states 'Be sure to change the storage replication type for a Recovery Services vault before you configure a backup in the vault. After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' The setting is found under Settings > Properties > Backup Configuration > Update, where you choose Geo-redundant (the default), Locally-redundant, or Zone-redundant. (a) is wrong: the option is disabled once backup is configured, and Azure Backup never migrates existing recovery points between replication types; moving from GRS to LRS requires stopping protection and deleting the data, or protecting the workload in a new LRS vault. (c) is wrong: it inverts the rule - completing a backup is exactly what locks the setting. (d) is wrong: the trigger is configuring a backup (creating a protected item), not the presence of policies. Every vault also contains default, system-managed backup policies that cannot be permanently deleted, so this condition could never be met.

domanda: You are preparing a new Recovery Services vault named RSV-Prod that will protect Azure virtual machines and SQL Server instances running in Azure VMs. No backups have been configured yet. Select the correct answer for each statement.
opzione_a: Default storage replication type of a newly created Recovery Services vault: [Locally-redundant | Geo-redundant | Zone-redundant]
opzione_b: The storage replication type of RSV-Prod can be modified: [At any time | Only before any backup is configured in the vault | Only after the first backup completes]
opzione_c: Vault type required to protect SQL Server running in an Azure VM: [Backup vault | Recovery Services vault | Either vault type]
opzione_d: The vault must be created in: [Any region in the subscription | The same region as the datasource | The paired region of the datasource]
risposta_corretta: Geo-redundant,Only before any backup is configured in the vault,Recovery Services vault,The same region as the datasource
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Geo-redundant: Microsoft Learn states that the storage replication type is by default set to geo-redundant storage (GRS), which is the default and recommended replication option; GRS replicates backup data to a secondary region hundreds of miles away. Locally-redundant and Zone-redundant are valid choices you can select, but neither is the default. Dropdown 2 - Only before any backup is configured in the vault: 'Be sure to change the storage replication type for a Recovery Services vault before you configure a backup in the vault. After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' 'At any time' and 'Only after the first backup completes' are wrong because configuring a backup permanently disables the control. Dropdown 3 - Recovery Services vault: SQL in Azure VM is listed as a Recovery Services vault datasource. A Backup vault supports only Azure Disks, Azure Blobs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL server, and Kubernetes services, so 'Backup vault' and 'Either vault type' are wrong. Dropdown 4 - The same region as the datasource: Learn states 'For you to create a vault to help protect any data source, the vault must be in the same region as the data source.' The Configure Backup wizard only lists VMs in the same region as the vault, so 'Any region' is wrong; the paired region is only used as a Cross Region Restore target, not as the vault location.
tags: recovery services vault,grs default,storage redundancy,sql in azure vm,vault region

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: A new Azure virtual machine named VM-Ledger hosts a financial application. The business requires a recovery point objective (RPO) of four hours. VM-Ledger is not yet protected by Azure Backup. You need to configure backup for VM-Ledger in an existing Recovery Services vault while meeting the RPO with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create a backup policy of subtype Standard and set the backup frequency to Hourly with an interval of every 4 hours.
opzione_b: Create a backup policy of subtype Enhanced with an Hourly schedule and a backup interval of every 4 hours, then assign it to VM-Ledger.
opzione_c: Create four Standard backup policies scheduled six hours apart and assign all of them to VM-Ledger.
opzione_d: Assign the default Standard policy to VM-Ledger and set the instant restore snapshot retention to 4 days.
spiegazione: Correct (b): Only the Enhanced backup policy subtype supports multiple backups per day for Azure VMs. With the schedule set to Hourly, you can choose an interval of 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours; hourly backup has a minimum RPO of 4 hours and a maximum of 24 hours. An Enhanced hourly policy with a 4-hour interval therefore meets the 4-hour RPO. (a) is wrong: the Standard policy does not offer an Hourly schedule - it backs up an Azure VM once a day, and Microsoft Learn states the minimum RPO with the Standard policy is 1 day (24 hours). (c) is wrong: a VM can be associated with only one backup policy in one vault at a time, so you cannot stack multiple policies on the same VM; it also would not reach a 4-hour RPO. (d) is wrong: instant restore snapshot retention controls how many days snapshots are kept in the snapshot tier for fast restores - it has no effect on backup frequency or RPO.
tags: backup policy,enhanced policy,standard policy,rpo,hourly backup,azure vm backup

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: Several Azure virtual machines are protected by a daily backup policy of subtype Standard. Restores are currently slow because snapshots expire too quickly, so the operations team asks you to keep instant restore snapshots for as long as the policy subtype allows. What is the maximum snapshot retention, in days, that you can configure on this policy?
spiegazione: Correct (b): For the Standard policy, Azure Backup retains Instant Restore snapshots locally for 2 days by default, and Microsoft Learn states you can configure this value from a minimum of 1 day to a maximum of 5 days. (a) is wrong: 2 days is the default value for the Standard policy, not the maximum. (c) is wrong: 7 days is the default snapshot retention for the Enhanced policy, not a value available to the Standard policy. (d) is wrong: 30 days is the maximum snapshot retention for the Enhanced policy (which supports 1 to 30 days, subject to the hourly frequency chosen); the Standard policy caps out at 5 days. Note also that Instant Restore cannot be disabled - the retention can only be reduced to a minimum of one day.
tags: instant restore,snapshot retention,standard policy,backup policy,snapshot tier

domanda: An auditor requires that your team be able to restore Azure VM backups into the Azure paired region on demand, to run compliance drills without waiting for Microsoft to declare a disaster in the primary region. You are creating a new Recovery Services vault for this workload. Which storage replication type must you select before you configure any backups?
spiegazione: Correct (c): Cross Region Restore (CRR) lets you restore data in a secondary Azure paired region at any time you choose, including for audit-compliance drills, without waiting for Azure to declare a disaster. Microsoft Learn states 'Cross Region Restore is supported only for a Recovery Services vault that uses the GRS replication type.' Because the replication type cannot be changed after backup is configured, Geo-redundant must be selected first. (a) is wrong: LRS keeps three copies within a single datacenter scale unit in the primary region - there is no secondary-region copy to restore from. (b) is wrong: ZRS replicates across availability zones within the same region, guaranteeing data residency; it enables Cross Zonal Restore, not Cross Region Restore. (d) is wrong: Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) is a real Azure Storage redundancy option, but the Recovery Services vault Backup Configuration pane offers only Geo-redundant, Locally-redundant, and Zone-redundant. Note that when CRR is enabled on a GRS vault, backup storage is upgraded to read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS).
tags: cross region restore,crr,grs,recovery services vault,storage redundancy,paired region

domanda: Your team is standardizing on the correct Azure Backup vault type per workload. Which datasources can be protected directly in a Recovery Services vault? Select all that apply.
opzione_b: SAP HANA running in an Azure VM
opzione_c: A container in an Azure Blob Storage account
opzione_d: An Azure Database for PostgreSQL server
spiegazione: Correct (a, b): Microsoft Learn lists the Recovery Services vault datasources as Azure Virtual Machine, SQL in Azure VM, Azure Files, SAP HANA in Azure VM, Azure Backup Server, Azure Backup agent (MARS), and DPM. Azure file shares (a) and SAP HANA in Azure VM (b) are both on that list. (c) is wrong: Azure Blobs are a Backup vault datasource. (d) is wrong: Azure Database for PostgreSQL server is a Backup vault datasource - it is in fact the workload Backup vaults were first introduced for. (e) is wrong: Azure Disks are a Backup vault datasource; standalone managed disks are protected through Azure Disk Backup, which uses a Backup vault and stores incremental snapshots in a snapshot resource group in your own subscription. Note the distinction from Azure VM backup, which protects the whole VM (including its disks) through a Recovery Services vault.
tags: recovery services vault,backup vault,datasources,azure files,sap hana,vault types

domanda: You must protect a standalone Azure managed disk named disk-data01 by using Azure Disk Backup. You plan to create the required vault, a backup policy, and a dedicated resource group that will hold the incremental snapshots. Select the correct answer for each statement.
opzione_a: Vault type you must create: [Recovery Services vault | Backup vault | Either vault type]
opzione_b: Recovery points created by Azure Disk Backup are stored in: [The operational (snapshot) tier only | The vault-standard tier only | Both the snapshot tier and the vault-standard tier]
opzione_c: Role to assign to the vault managed identity on disk-data01: [Disk Backup Reader | Disk Snapshot Contributor | Storage Blob Data Contributor]
opzione_d: Role to assign to the vault managed identity on the snapshot resource group: [Disk Backup Reader | Disk Snapshot Contributor | Backup Contributor]
risposta_corretta: Backup vault,The operational (snapshot) tier only,Disk Backup Reader,Disk Snapshot Contributor
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - Backup vault: Azure Disks are a Backup vault datasource; Recovery Services vaults do not support standalone managed disks, so 'Recovery Services vault' and 'Either vault type' are wrong. Dropdown 2 - The operational (snapshot) tier only: Microsoft Learn states 'Azure Disk backup supports only the operational tier backup. Copying of backups to the vault storage tier is currently not supported.' Consequently the Backup vault storage redundancy setting (LRS/GRS) does not apply to these recovery points - incremental snapshots are stored on Standard HDD storage in your snapshot resource group, and on ZRS by default in ZRS-supported regions. The other two options describe Azure VM backup behaviour, not Disk Backup. Dropdown 3 - Disk Backup Reader: Learn states 'Assign the Disk Backup Reader role to Backup Vault's managed identity on the Source disk that needs to be backed up.' Storage Blob Data Contributor is a data-plane role for blob storage and is irrelevant here. Dropdown 4 - Disk Snapshot Contributor: Learn states 'Assign the Disk Snapshot Contributor role to the Backup vault's managed identity on the Resource group where backups are created and managed by the Azure Backup service.' Disk Backup Reader belongs on the source disk, and Backup Contributor is a Recovery Services vault management role, not a snapshot-datastore role.
tags: azure disk backup,backup vault,operational tier,disk backup reader,disk snapshot contributor,managed identity

domanda:
Fabrikam creates a Recovery Services vault named RSV1 in the East US region by accepting all the default settings, and immediately configures backup for 10 Azure virtual machines. The compliance team now asks whether restores can be triggered in the paired region on demand, and the finance team asks whether backup storage costs can be lowered. For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
1. You can change the storage replication type of RSV1 from Geo-redundant to Locally-redundant on the vault's Backup Configuration pane.
2. Because RSV1 uses the default replication type, Cross Region Restore can be enabled on RSV1.
3. Enabling Cross Region Restore on RSV1 upgrades the vault's backup storage to read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS).
opzione_a: You can change the storage replication type of RSV1 from Geo-redundant to Locally-redundant on the vault's Backup Configuration pane.
opzione_b: Because RSV1 uses the default replication type, Cross Region Restore can be enabled on RSV1.
opzione_c: Enabling Cross Region Restore on RSV1 upgrades the vault's backup storage to read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS).
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: Backup was already configured for the 10 VMs. Microsoft Learn states 'Be sure to change the storage replication type for a Recovery Services vault before you configure a backup in the vault. After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' To actually move to LRS, Fabrikam must either stop protection and delete the data in the GRS vault and reconfigure backup in a new LRS vault, or stop protection with retained data and protect the VMs in a new LRS vault (which requires moving each VM to another resource group and paying to keep the old recovery points). Statement 2 - Yes: The default (and recommended) storage replication type for a new Recovery Services vault is Geo-redundant, and Cross Region Restore is supported only for a Recovery Services vault that uses the GRS replication type. CRR is enabled at the vault level under Properties > Backup Configuration > Cross Region Restore > Enable; after enabling it, backup items can take up to 48 hours to become available in the secondary region. Statement 3 - Yes: The Azure Backup glossary states 'For GRS vaults that have the cross-region restore feature enabled, backup storage is upgraded from GRS to RA-GRS (Read-Access Geo-Redundant Storage).' This is what allows reads from the secondary region without Azure declaring a disaster, and it incurs extra charges.
tags: recovery services vault,storage redundancy,cross region restore,ra-grs,grs to lrs

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: You must protect a Trusted Launch virtual machine named VM-TL01 that runs in the West Europe region. The backup data must remain resilient to a single availability zone failure while guaranteeing data residency within West Europe, and the VM must be backed up multiple times per day. No Recovery Services vault exists yet. Drag the four actions into the correct sequence.
opzione_a: Configure backup for VM-TL01 and assign the Enhanced policy.
opzione_b: Create a Recovery Services vault in the West Europe region.
opzione_c: On the vault's Backup Configuration pane, set the storage replication type to Zone-redundant.
opzione_d: Create a backup policy of subtype Enhanced with an Hourly schedule.
spiegazione: Correct order: b, c, d, a. Step 1 (b): The vault must exist first, and it must be in the same region as the datasource - Microsoft Learn states 'For you to create a vault to help protect any data source, the vault must be in the same region as the data source', and the Configure Backup wizard only lists VMs in the same region as the vault. Step 2 (c): Zone-redundant storage replicates backup data across availability zones, guaranteeing backup data residency and resiliency within the same region, which matches the stated requirement. This must be set before any backup is configured, because 'After you configure a backup, the option to modify is disabled.' Placing this step after configuring backup would make the requirement unachievable in this vault. Step 3 (d): The policy must exist before it can be assigned. The Enhanced subtype is required here for two reasons: Trusted Launch VM backup is configured through Enhanced policies in the portal, and only the Enhanced policy supports multiple backups per day (Hourly schedules with intervals of 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours). Step 4 (a): Configuring backup and assigning the policy creates the protected item and triggers the initial backup - and it is this action that locks the storage replication type, which is why it must come last.
tags: recovery services vault,zrs,zone-redundant,enhanced policy,trusted launch,backup policy,ordering

domanda: Six months ago, an administrator created a Recovery Services vault named RSV-Legacy with the default settings and configured backup for 40 Azure virtual machines. An on-premises tape system is the company's primary backup endpoint, so Azure backup storage costs must now be reduced by moving the vault's backup data to locally-redundant storage. The existing recovery points do not need to be preserved. What should you do?
opzione_a: In RSV-Legacy, open Properties > Backup Configuration > Update and set the storage replication type to Locally-redundant.
opzione_b: Run Set-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProperty and set the BackupStorageRedundancy parameter of RSV-Legacy to LocallyRedundant.
opzione_c: Disable soft delete on RSV-Legacy, stop protection and delete the backup data for the 40 VMs, create a new vault configured for Locally-redundant storage, and reconfigure backup for the VMs in the new vault.
opzione_d: Move RSV-Legacy to a new resource group, then set the storage replication type to Locally-redundant during the move operation.
spiegazione: Correct (c): Once a backup is configured in a Recovery Services vault, the storage replication type can no longer be modified, and Azure Backup cannot migrate existing recovery points between replication types or move backup data to a different vault. Microsoft Learn's documented workaround, when previous backup data does not need to be preserved, is to disable soft delete in the GRS vault, stop protection and delete the backups from the existing vault, and then configure backups for the workload in a new LRS vault. Disabling soft delete is required first, because otherwise deleted backup data is retained in a soft-deleted state. (a) is wrong: the Update control on the Backup Configuration pane is disabled after a backup has been configured, so this cannot be performed in the portal. (b) is wrong: the same service-side restriction applies to Az PowerShell, the CLI, and the REST API - the limitation is not a portal UI limitation, so the cmdlet fails for a vault with protected items. (d) is wrong: moving a vault between resource groups or subscriptions is supported, but it has no effect on the storage replication type and does not unlock the setting.
tags: recovery services vault,grs to lrs,storage redundancy,soft delete,stop protection,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: You are evaluating whether to adopt the Enhanced backup policy subtype for Azure virtual machine backups in a Recovery Services vault. Which three statements about the Enhanced policy are correct? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select all that apply.
opzione_a: The backup schedule can be set to Hourly with an interval of 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours.
opzione_b: Instant Restore snapshot retention can be configured up to 30 days.
opzione_c: Backup and instant restore of Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks are supported.
opzione_d: After a VM is protected with an Enhanced policy, the policy type can be changed back to Standard.
opzione_e: The Enhanced policy writes recovery points only to the vault-standard tier and does not create local snapshots.
spiegazione: Correct (a, b, c): (a) With the Enhanced policy the backup schedule can be Hourly, Daily, or Weekly; for Hourly you can set the backup schedule to 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 hours, giving a minimum RPO of 4 hours and a maximum of 24 hours. (b) The Enhanced policy allows Instant Restore snapshot retention from 1 to 30 days, with a default of 7 days - versus 1 to 5 days (default 2) for the Standard policy. The exact maximum depends on the hourly frequency chosen, because a higher snapshot count per day reduces the maximum allowed days, and instant restore retention cannot exceed the vault retention duration. (c) Microsoft Learn states the Enhanced policy supports backup and instant restore of Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks, in addition to Standard HDD, Standard SSD, and Premium SSD v1 - the Standard policy does not support these newer offerings. (d) is wrong: Learn states 'Backup doesn't allow changing the policy type to Standard after you enable a VM backup with the Enhanced policy.' (e) is wrong: this describes the opposite of Instant Restore, which is enabled for everyone and cannot be disabled. The Enhanced policy uses managed disk snapshots stored alongside the disks for Instant Restore (the initial snapshot is a full copy, subsequent ones are incremental), in addition to the copy transferred to the vault-standard tier.
tags: enhanced policy,backup policy,instant restore,ultra disk,premium ssd v2,hourly backup

sotto_argomento: Create and configure a backup policy
domanda: You are authoring a grandfather-father-son (GFS) backup policy of subtype Standard for the Azure virtual machines of a regulated business unit. The policy takes one backup per day, and the retention requirements for daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly recovery points are still being negotiated with the compliance team. Select the correct answer for each statement.
opzione_a: Maximum Instant Restore snapshot retention configurable on this policy: [2 days | 5 days | 7 days | 30 days]
opzione_b: Minimum retention range supported for a daily backup point: [1 day | 7 days | 30 days]
opzione_c: Maximum retention configurable for daily recovery points: [180 days | 372 days | 9999 days]
opzione_d: The Instant Restore snapshot retention compared with the vault retention duration: [Can exceed it | Cannot exceed it | Must be identical to it]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 5 days: For the Standard policy, the default snapshot retention is 2 days and it is configurable from a minimum of 1 day to a maximum of 5 days. 7 days is the Enhanced policy default and 30 days is the Enhanced policy maximum, so neither is available on a Standard policy. (Note: for weekly Standard policies the snapshot retention is fixed at 5 days.) Dropdown 2 - 7 days: Microsoft Learn states 'Azure Virtual Machine backup policy supports a minimum retention range from seven days up to 9999 days', and any modification to an existing VM backup policy with less than seven days requires an update to meet the seven-day minimum. 1 day is the Instant Restore snapshot minimum, not the vault retention minimum. Dropdown 3 - 9999 days: The documented maximum retentions for Azure VM backup points are 9999 days (daily), 5163 weeks (weekly), 1188 months (monthly), and 99 years (yearly). 180 days is only the default daily vault retention, and 372 days is the number of days a 12-month monthly retention actually covers (Azure Backup counts 31 days per month, so 31 x 12 = 372). Dropdown 4 - Cannot exceed it: Learn states 'Instant restore retention duration cannot exceed vault retention duration', and the retention model does not allow deleting the vault restore point (tier 2) unless the snapshot (tier 1) is deleted - Microsoft therefore recommends scheduling a vault retention period greater than the snapshot retention period.
tags: gfs,backup policy,retention,instant restore,snapshot retention,azure vm backup
